verdict: The Turkish content here is genuinely good – the address system (abi/abla/amca/teyze, Bey/Hanım after the first name), the courtesy layer (Buyurun, Kolay gelsin, Geçmiş olsun, Eline sağlık, Hoş geldiniz), the register calls (niye over niçin, mesela over örneğin, Gitmem lazım over Gitmeliyim, satın almak demoted, -maktadır absent) and the food substitutions (börek for samosa, gözleme for paratha, tereyağı for ghee, karpuz for mango) are all right, and the false-friend catches at hs-0861 pasta and hs-0909 daire are worth real money. The failures are concentrated and they are structural. First, the Hindi spine's blind spots are wide open: there is no item anywhere for the yes/no question word mı/mi/mu/mü, the one thing that turns any Turkish sentence into a question and the single largest omission in the list – it appears inside a dozen chunks and is never taught; likewise no item for vowel harmony (invoked in twenty notes, defined in none), none for verb-final word order or the absence of articles, none for the seven letters English lacks (the app gives Turkish no script teacher, so pronunciation has nowhere else to live), none for the definite-object rule that decides between kitap okudum and kitabı okudum, none for the noun+noun -(s)i compound that builds half the menu the syllabus already lists as vocabulary, none for p ç t k softening, and none for the -mek istiyorum frame. Second, whole daily domains are missing rather than mis-tiered: no İyi günler, no Hoşça kalın/Güle güle, no Hoş bulduk, no Rica ederim, no inşallah or maşallah – all of them present only inside other items' notes or absent entirely – plus no kebap, no döner, no beer, wine or rakı anywhere in 1,154 items aimed at a British adult, no tane, no artık, no zaten, no nereye, and no -li/-siz despite hs-0792's own note calling it 'vital for ordering'. Third, tier inversions where a chunk outranks the paradigm it depends on: tier-1 'Bakar mısınız?' rests on a tier-2 aorist, tier-1 -ebilmek is followed by a tier-2 '-ebilir miyim?' that its own note calls the most useful frame in the language, and the tier-1 copula cannot be negated because değil sits at tier 2. Fourth, and this is the housekeeping that most needs a script rather than an author: roughly sixty duplicate pairs and triples (Buyurun 0086/0443, Geçmiş olsun 0348/0785, üstünde, karşısında, Görüşürüz, anne, baba, aile, teyze, amca, pişirmek, dolmuş, pazar, saat ×3, acı ×3, kullanmak ×3, Susadım, tuvalet, hâlâ, biri, dinlenmek, Gitmem lazım, eğer…-se, -ince), several of them carrying contradictory tiers (kayınvalide 3 vs 5, amca 1 vs 3, teyze 1 vs 2, biri 2 vs 3); eight of the sixteen tier-6 'N/A' slots are not language gaps at all but the syllabus's own duplicates relabelled (hs-0821 Pazar, hs-0847 akşam yemeği, hs-1086 sıfır, hs-1117 vantilatör, hs-1135 hastane, hs-1151 kullanmak), while two are outright wrong – hs-0780 marks the ordinary pronoun onlar N/A and so never teaches 'they' at all despite teaching onlara, onların and onlardan, and hs-0568 claims no second word for table when sofra is one and the syllabus already uses it; and the tier-6 placeholder is sometimes an en dash, sometimes an em dash (against house style), sometimes the real word. The roman field is a systemic defect: identical to the word for the first ~730 items, then ASCII-folded from roughly hs-0773 to the end (Gecmis olsun, Gunaydin, tesekkur, Sarjim bitti, gozluk), so the same phrase carries two different roman values in two places, hâlâ collides exactly with hala 'paternal aunt', and the folding erases the ş/s, ı/i and ü/u distinctions that are phonemic in Turkish – for a Latin-script language roman should simply equal word, everywhere. One flat error to fix before anything ships: hs-0025 teaches that the de/da linker hardens to 'te' ('Mehmet te geldi'). It never does – that is the locative suffix, and the non-hardening of the linker is the best-known spelling rule in Turkish.

items.note: Turkish has no word for 'is' – the predicate just sits there: Bu güzel = this is nice. var/yok is the existence pair.
'not' before a noun or adjective is değil (Bu pahalı değil); verbs negate with -me-/-ma-. A head-tilt plus 'yok' does most refusing in speech.
'he' and 'hı hı' are the casual yeahs; tamam = okay, fine.
Copula ending: İngiliz misiniz? = are you English? Harmony: -sınız/-siniz/-sunuz/-sünüz.
Ben İngiliz'im, hazırım, açım. Harmony: -ım/-im/-um/-üm; -yım after a vowel.
One word for he/she/it – Turkish has no gender at all.
Marked twice: Ali'nin evi = Ali's house, otobüs durağı = bus stop. Harmony: -in/-ın/-un/-ün, -nin after a vowel.
Evde = at home, masada = on the table. Hardens to -te/-ta after p ç t k f s ş h: markette.
Eve gidiyorum = I'm going home; bana = to me. The definite-object marker is separate: -i/-ı/-u/-ü.
İngiltere'den = from England. Hardens to -ten/-tan. 'with' is a different suffix: -le/-la.
Plain -de already covers 'on' (masada = on the table); üstünde stresses physically on top of.
Speech often prefers -le/-la for 'and' between people: Ali'yle ben = Ali and me. 'more' is daha.
Turkish has no topic particle like Hindi's तो; 'as for me' is bence or bana kalırsa.
Nasılsın? = how are you? Harmony: -sın/-sin/-sun/-sün.
The all-purpose polite noise: answering your name, answering the phone, asking someone to repeat.
selam = hi (casual); günaydın = good morning; iyi günler as you leave a shop.
güzel = nice, lovely; 'İyi, iyi' also works as 'right, I see'.
Written as a separate word and harmonised: ben de, o da. Unlike the locative -de, the linker NEVER hardens – it is always 'Mehmet de geldi', never 'te'. 'even' is bile.

items.en: to be; to become; to happen

items.note: Stem hardens before a vowel: gidiyorum, gideceğim.

items.en: aorist: general habits, offers and willingness – Çay içerim = I drink tea
items.note: Spoken Turkish uses -iyor for both 'I do' and 'I'm doing'; the aorist is for habits, offers (Çay içer misiniz?) and 'Olur' = that works.
Marked on the noun: evim = my house; the pronoun benim is usually dropped.
Adınız = your name, eviniz = your house.
Bana su lazım = I need water. Irregular: ben + -e gives bana, not bene.
Same stem takes the cases: nereye = where to, nereden = where from. In speech it often sounds 'nerde'.
neden is the neutral twin, niçin the bookish one; all three are said.
Counted noun stays singular: kaç kişi? = how many people? For amounts and prices use ne kadar.
buraya = to here, buradan = from here; often shortened to 'burda'.
şurada = just over there (pointing).
az önce = just now, a moment ago; hemen = right away.
Hindi's single kal splits in two here: yarın = tomorrow, dün = yesterday.
'again' is tekrar or yine.
fazla = too much, excessive; bir daha = once more.
Bu kadar yeter = that'll do. Refusing more tea: 'Yeter, sağ olun'.
herkes = everyone; bütün or tüm before a noun: bütün gün = all day.
Said 'bişey'. In negatives: bir şey yok = there's nothing.
birisi is the same word; in negatives switch to kimse: kimse yok = there's nobody.
millet = the public, folk (colloquial); adamlar = the blokes.

items.en: matter; subject; the thing we're talking about
items.note: laf = talk, idle words; söz = one's word, a promise.
Ne iş yapıyorsunuz? = what do you do for a living?
Nearly always with a possessive: adım, adınız, ismi. The i drops: isim becomes ismi.
Black, in a tulip glass, no milk. 'açık' = weak, 'demli' = strong.
Same word for the noun and the verb, exactly like Hindi khana.
vakit is the everyday twin: vaktim yok = I haven't got time. saat = clock time.
Also the universal hesitation word, like English 'thingy'.

items.en: to take; to buy; to get

items.note: bakmak = to look at (…-e bakmak); izlemek = to watch.
duymak = to hear.
Ne dedin? = what did you say? 'Ne demek?' = what does that mean, and also 'not at all' after thanks.
tanışmak = to meet for the first time – 'Memnun oldum' = nice to meet you; bulmak = to find.
Haberin var mı? = have you heard about it? adres = address, the other half of Hindi pata.
'to live, reside' is oturmak: Nerede oturuyorsunuz?
Bana bir taksi lazım. gerek is the neutral twin; -meli on the verb = should.
Yürüyerek gidelim = let's walk it; yürüyerek ne kadar sürer? = how long on foot?
yapmak already covers 'make': yemek yapmak = to cook a meal, and that is what people say.

items.en: imperative levels: bare stem for sen, stem + -in for siz, -iniz for extra formality
items.note: Gel / gelin, otur / oturun, bak / bakın. The -iniz form is signs-and-officials register.
hadi on its own = come on; -(y)elim on any verb = let's.

items.en: come in; after you; go ahead; here you are
items.note: The single most useful courtesy word in Turkey. At the door it pairs with Hoş geldiniz (welcome), answered with Hoş bulduk.
Warmer full version: 'Buyurun, oturun'. To a friend: otur.
On the phone or at a counter you will simply hear 'Buyurun?'
The everyday one, borrowed from French. Affedersiniz is the fuller version.
Kusura bakmayın = sorry, no offence meant.
Used far less than English 'please' – a polite verb form usually carries the courtesy on its own.
Bir şey değil = you're welcome, after teşekkürler. Önemli değil = it doesn't matter.
For a customer, a boss or an elder; plain evet is the everyday norm.
You will need it two or three times before the tea stops coming.
To a friend: Nasılsın?
Full reflex: 'İyiyim, sağ olun, siz nasılsınız?'
No verb needed. 'Bu nedir?' is the written or formal version, not a politer one – to be polite you soften the whole question: 'Affedersiniz, bu ne?'
Usually just 'Adım Tom'.
To a friend: Adın ne?
Literally 'I've got hungry'. 'Açım' works too.
Pattern: verb + -mem lazım. 'Gitmem gerek' is identical in meaning.
fakat is the written twin.
veya is the neutral written one; in questions: 'Çay mı kahve mi?'
'Aa!' is the pure surprise noise; 'yahu' is 'oh come off it'.
Teens and tens just stack: on bir = 11, yirmi = 20, otuz = 30, kırk = 40, elli = 50.
Turks always say which: abi = older brother, abla = older sister, erkek/kız kardeş for younger ones.
An older sister is abla, never kız kardeş.
Used to sons and to younger men, exactly like Hindi beta. Root: oğul.

items.en: my daughter; love (to a younger woman)
items.note: Root kız = girl, daughter.

items.en: older sister; 'love' to a woman a bit older than you
items.note: The standard friendly address for a woman in a shop or on the street.

items.en: older brother; 'mate' to a man a bit older than you
items.note: Written ağabey, always said abi. Taxi drivers, waiters, shopkeepers: abi.

items.en: may it come easy (said to anyone who's working)
items.note: Turkish has no 'have you eaten?' greeting. This is the everyday act of care: said to a driver, a waiter, a shopkeeper, a builder.
Turks say 'I know Turkish' (biliyorum), not 'I speak'.
Or 'Biraz yavaş, lütfen'.
'Bir daha söyler misiniz?' is just as common; 'Efendim?' alone = sorry, what?

items.en: how do you say this in Turkish?
items.note: Also 'Buna Türkçe ne deniyor?'
-ce/-ca makes any language: İngilizce, Almanca, Fransızca.
Follows the plain noun: senin için = for you, bunun için = for this.
In speech it sticks on: benimle, seninle, Ali'yle, otobüsle = by bus.

items.en: to have (Arabam var = I have a car)
items.note: There is no verb 'to have': the thing owned takes a possessive suffix and var (or yok) follows.
Gidebilirim = I can go; 'Alabilir miyim?' = may I have…? Negative is different: gidemem = I can't go.
hızlı = fast; erken = early; 'Acelem var' = I'm in a hurry.
Saat üç = three o'clock; saat üçte = at three.

items.en: aunty (mum's sister, and any older woman)
items.note: hala = dad's sister. As an address, teyze is the warm word for an older woman.

items.en: uncle (dad's brother, and any older man)
items.note: dayı = mum's brother, also 'geezer' affectionately.
Everyday speech just says çocuk (kid); oğlan is the blunt colloquial word.
'Bir çay getirir misiniz?' = could you bring a tea?

items.en: to close; to switch off; to hang up
items.note: kapalı = closed, kapı = door.
Only on the phone – never face to face.

items.en: to ring, to call; to look for
items.note: 'Seni ararım' = I'll ring you. Same verb as 'to search for'.
Plain talking is konuşmak; sohbet is the sitting-with-tea kind.
Comes with everything; 'pide' is the flat one, 'simit' the sesame ring.
pirinç = uncooked rice; bulgur pilavı is just as common.
The everyday staple, like dal: mercimek çorbası = lentil soup.
On a lokanta counter, the veg dishes are the 'zeytinyağlılar' (in olive oil) and 'sulu yemek'.
Never in tea. 'sütlü kahve' if you want a white coffee.
acısız = without chilli; baharatlı = spiced but not hot.
A whole spread of cheese, olives, tomato and eggs. Literally 'before coffee'.
At a Turkish table you'll hear this until you say Doydum.

items.en: the food's lovely (lit. health to your hand)
items.note: Said to whoever cooked. Formal: Elinize sağlık. The reply is 'Afiyet olsun'.
'Boş odanız var mı?' = have you got a room free?
banyo = bathroom for washing; signs say WC (said 've-ce') or lavabo.
TL for short; kuruş is the small change nobody uses.
'Kaça?' and 'Kaç para?' are just as common in a market.
To a friend: Dur. Getting out of a dolmuş: 'Müsait bir yerde inecek var'.

items.en: I liked it (lit. it went to my liking)
items.note: Present: hoşuma gidiyor = I like it. beğendim does the same job.

items.en: I wonder; by any chance (softens a question)
items.note: 'Acaba bir bakabilir miyim?' = could I possibly have a look?
Türk = a Turk; Türkiye'de = in Turkey.
bavul = suitcase, çanta = bag, bagaj = luggage at the airport.

items.en: copula endings: İngiliz'im, İngiliz misin?, İngiliz, hazırız, hazır mısınız?
items.note: Third person takes nothing at all: 'O İngiliz'. Negative uses değil: 'Hazır değilim'.
'Olur' = fine by me, that works.
The neutral everyday one. 'Mersi' is the French loan you'll also hear.
Said before, during and after eating, and back to anyone who thanks the cook.
Bir çay istiyorum. Softer in a shop: 'Bir çay alabilir miyim?'
sevmek = to like/love generally; hoşuna gitmek = to appeal to someone.
'Bilmem' = dunno; 'Hiçbir fikrim yok' = no idea at all.
'Do you know English' is the Turkish phrasing.
Literally 'of where are you'. The follow-up is always 'Memleket neresi?' = where's home originally?
Or 'İngiltere'denim' = I'm from England.
Otogar nerede? Metro nerede? No verb needed.
Just 'ben' plus your name. 'Kimsiniz?' = who's calling?
'Bir saniye' is just as common.
'İmdat!' is the emergency shout.
The one leaving says 'Hoşça kalın'; the one staying says 'Güle güle'.
Polite: Kendinize iyi bakın.
The constant Turkish offer. Polite: 'Çay içer misiniz?' or 'Ne içersiniz?'
patates kızartması = chips.

items.en: two-level politeness: sen for friends, children and peers; siz for strangers, elders and anyone official
items.note: No third level. Using sen to an older stranger is the classic tourist slip; wait to be offered it.
The warm everyday thanks. Literally 'be healthy'.
Turkish points three ways: bu = this, şu = that one there (pointing), o = that/it (already known).
yine = again, once more of the same; bir daha = one more time.
Invariable – no matter the verb or person, it's always değil mi.
'Acısız olsun' does the same. Turkish food is mostly mild anyway – the chilli flakes are on the table.
Turks say annem/babam with the possessive, not bare anne. '-ciğim' adds warmth: anneciğim.

items.en: Bey and Hanım follow the FIRST name to show respect
items.note: Never the surname. For strangers slightly older: abi and abla; for the elderly: amca and teyze. Fully formal: Beyefendi, Hanımefendi.
Açım = I'm hungry; tok = full. Same spelling as 'aç!' = open it.
Bende para yok = I've no money on me; 'Bende kalsın' = keep it, leave it with me.
The negative of var, and a casual 'no'. For 'is not' with a noun or adjective use değil: Bu pahalı değil.

items.en: that one / this one (pointing at food or goods)
items.note: 'Şundan bir tane' = one of those, please.
To a friend: 'Baksana'. Never click or wave.
Turkish normally builds these with a verbal noun instead: 'Geldiğini biliyorum' = I know that he came. ki is the spoken shortcut: 'Biliyorum ki…'
Otursana = do sit down; baksana = have a look, will you.

items.en: present: yapıyorum = I'm doing / I do
items.note: Covers both English presents, so learn it before the aorist. Stem-final e/a becomes i/ı: gelmek gives geliyor, anlamak gives anlıyor.

items.en: past copula: hastaydım = I was ill, güzeldi = it was lovely
items.note: Existence: vardı = there was, yoktu = there wasn't.
onun evi, or just evi. No gender to worry about.
Bizim ev = our house is the everyday shortcut.
Nasıl bir yer? = what sort of place is it? Nothing agrees – Turkish adjectives never change.
Hangi otobüs? = which bus? hangisi = which one.
Days: pazartesi, salı, çarşamba, perşembe, cuma, cumartesi, pazar.
anlatmak = to tell, relate, explain at length.
'Bir şey sorabilir miyim?' = can I ask you something?
Ne kadar sürer? = how long does it take? For 'it seems', Turkish uses '… gibi geliyor'.
uyanmak = to wake up; 'İyi uykular' = sleep well.
Nerede oturuyorsunuz? = where do you live?

items.en: to get up; to depart (bus, train)
items.note: 'Otobüs kaçta kalkıyor?' = what time does the bus leave?

items.en: not: gitme! = don't go; bilmiyorum = I don't know
items.note: One negative suffix does everything, slotted straight after the verb stem. Polite command: yapmayın.
Or simply 'Bir çay, lütfen'.
Pardon is the quicker everyday version.
'Çok teşekkür ederim' for real gratitude.
'İyi misin?' = are you okay?
Said 'naber' among friends. Also 'Ne var ne yok?'; the stock reply is 'İyilik sağlık'.

items.en: I like … (Çay severim = I like tea)
items.note: Aorist for general liking; 'çok sevdim' = I really liked it (this one time).
The -se/-sa goes on the verb and eğer is optional: 'Yağmur yağarsa' = if it rains.
The commonest filler in spoken Turkish, and genuinely useful for buying thinking time.

items.en: there you go; that's just it
items.note: 'İşte bu!' = that's the one. Turkish has no ही particle; işte does the pinning-down.
kendi evim = my own house; kendim = myself; 'Kendine iyi bak'.
Slightly formal; 'Görüşürüz' is what you'll actually say.

items.en: until; up to; as much as
items.note: Takes the dative: akşama kadar = until evening; 'bu kadar' = this much.

items.en: witnessed past: geldim = I came, gitti = he went
items.note: Hardens after voiceless consonants: gitti, baktım. Turkish has nothing like Hindi's ने – the subject never changes shape.

items.en: future: yapacağım = I'll do it, gelecek = he'll come
items.note: In speech it contracts hard: yapacağım sounds 'yapıcam', gideceğim 'gidicem'. The -iyor present also covers the near future.

items.word: ev / evi / eve / evde / evden / evin
items.roman: ev / evi / eve / evde / evden / evin
items.en: case endings: house / the house (object) / to the house / at the house / from the house / of the house
items.note: This is the spine of Turkish and it comes early, not late. All six harmonise with the last vowel: göz, gözü, göze, gözde, gözden, gözün.
Bakayım = let me have a look; Gidelim mi? = shall we go?

items.en: the one that: benimki = mine, masadaki = the one on the table
items.note: Attaches to a case-marked or possessed word: benimki = mine, masadaki = the one on the table, dünkü = yesterday's. It does not harmonise with a/ı.
Bundan daha ucuz = cheaper than this. Often just 'daha ucuz'.
en güzel = the nicest, en yakın = the nearest.
'Tamamdır' = all sorted; 'Olmadı' = it didn't work; 'Olur' = fine by me.
'Sanırım' = I reckon; 'Bana kalırsa' = if you ask me.
'Gitmem lazım' is the more spoken version.
The -abilir mi pattern is the polite request workhorse.
Üç gün önce = three days ago; 'Önce ben' = me first.
'Birazdan' = in a little while; plain 'sonra' usually does.
Yemekten sonra = after the meal.
Saat beşten önce = before five.
'hep' is the short spoken one: hep aynı = always the same.
Hiç gitmedim = I've never been. The verb still has to be negative. 'asla' = never, emphatic.
Noun stays singular: her gün, her şey, her yer.
'Başka bir şey?' = anything else? ikinci = second; diğeri = the other one.
Doubles up with a negative verb: 'Hiçbir şey istemiyorum'.
Two words, though people say it as one.
Answer with -de: 'Saat üçte' = at three.
Same word as clock and o'clock (hs-0140) – Turkish uses one for all three.
'sene' is just as common in speech.
Günaydın = good morning; 'sabah sabah' = first thing in the morning.
'İyi akşamlar' = good evening.
'İyi geceler' = goodnight.
'Evvelsi gün' or 'önceki gün' = the day before yesterday. Turkish splits what Hindi does with one word.
Also 'face'. iki yüz = 200 (never 'bir yüz').
iki bin = 2000; also 'get on!' (binmek).
yarım = half of one; buçuk = the half after a whole number: bir buçuk, saat üç buçuk = half three.
'ilk' is the everyday one: ilk defa = the first time.
'kocam' = my husband. 'eşim' = my spouse, the neutral polite choice.
'karım' = my wife is normal, but bare 'karı' about a woman is rude. eş works for either sex.
'kaynana' is the everyday word, with all the same jokes attached.
'kayınbaba' colloquially.

items.en: brother's or uncle's wife; a mate's wife
items.note: Warm and very commonly used as an address.
Plural is just -lar/-ler by vowel harmony: çocuklar, evler. Dropped after a number: iki çocuk.
evlilik = marriage; 'Evli misiniz?' = are you married? is asked within five minutes.
Everyday speech just uses almak (hs-0069): 'Bunu aldım' = I bought this.
Also 'to sing' a song, and 'Ne okuyorsun?' = what are you studying?
'yollamak' is the more casual one.

items.en: to go out; to set off; to come out
items.note: 'Ben çıkıyorum' = I'm off. Also 'to go out with' someone.
gelmek does most of this work: 'Saat üçte geliriz'.
Takes the dative: 'Size yardım edebilir miyim?' = can I help you?
To try TO do something is çalışmak: 'anlamaya çalışıyorum' = I'm trying to understand.
Takes the dative: 'Yağmur yağmaya başladı'.

items.en: it's finished; it's over; we've run out
items.note: In a shop 'Bitti' means they've none left. bitirmek = to finish something.
Polite: 'Sesiniz gelmiyor'. 'Çekmiyor' = there's no signal; 'kopuyor' = you're breaking up.
Polite or plural: Sizi özledim.
Ordering tea or coffee: sade = no sugar, orta = medium, şekerli = sweet.
Also 'sweet' of a person: 'Çok tatlısın'.
'Karnım aç' = I'm hungry; 'Midem bulanıyor' = I feel sick.
The only reliable way to stop the refills. 'Çok doydum' if they carry on.
In Istanbul: metro, tramvay, Marmaray and the vapur (ferry).
'otogar' = the coach station for intercity buses.

items.en: shared minibus taxi on a fixed route
items.note: Turkey's answer to the auto-rickshaw: pay as you board, money passed forward. In Istanbul often called minibüs. A normal cab is a taksi.
In Istanbul you tap an İstanbulkart instead.
durak = the stop; otogar = coach station; iskele = ferry pier.
'market' = the corner shop; 'bakkal' = the little grocer's.
Also Sunday. 'çarşı' = the shopping quarter; Kapalıçarşı = the Grand Bazaar.
'İyi yolculuklar' = have a good trip.
'Düz gidin, sonra sağa sapın'. sağ = right, sol = left.
'Çok pahalı!' is the opening move when haggling in a bazaar.
For people use yaşlı; eski about a person means 'ex-'.
'ılık' = lukewarm.

items.en: broken; out of order; (of food) off
items.note: 'kötü' = bad. 'Bozuk paranız var mı?' = have you got any change?
'Haklısın' = you're right (about a view); 'yanlış' = wrong.
'Memnun oldum' = pleased to meet you; 'keyfim yerinde' = I'm in good spirits.
kirli or pis = dirty.
'Hazır mısınız?' = are you ready?

Bunun fiyatı ne? = what's the price of this?
Beni ara = call me; bana is 'to me'
Onunla = with him/her
Başka bir şey = something else
Henüz is 'yet' in negatives: henüz gelmedi
Örneğin is slightly more formal

items.word: ne-/bu-/şu-/o- grid: nerede–burada–şurada–orada, ne zaman–şimdi–o zaman, nasıl–böyle–şöyle–öyle, kim–bu–şu–o
items.note: Turkish points three ways: bu (here by me), şu (just there), o (over there)
Otelin önünde buluşalım
Also of time: akşama doğru
Plural -ler on a name means that person's household
Comparison takes the ablative: benden az
Also 'or' in questions: çay mı yoksa kahve mi?
Kesinlikle hayır = absolutely not
Galiba kayboldum = I think I'm lost; sanırım does the same
Sağ ol / sağ olun is the everyday shorter thanks
Polite: kusura bakmayın; özür dilerim = I apologise
Bak informally; Bak ne diyeceğim = listen, here's the thing
Fazla alone = too much/extra
Bütün gün = all day; hepsi = all of it
Passive -ıl/-in: yapmak to yapılmak. For 'become', olmak.
Also gitmem gerekiyor; gitmek zorundayım = I'm forced to
Hazırım = I'm ready
Yola çıktım = I've set off
Dönmek alone also means 'to turn'
Yemeye çıkalım = let's go out to eat
Kar yağıyor = it's snowing
Rezervasyon yaptırmak is the formal version
Lit. to look at the phone; telefonu açmak works too
The extra mode a visitor really needs, and it takes the same İstanbulkart as the metro and the bus. iskele = the pier.
Tramvay, metrobüs and füniküler take the same card
Sırt çantası = rucksack
Trafik çok sıkışık = the traffic is heavy

Yürüyerek ne kadar sürer? = how long on foot?
Rötar = a transport delay; gecikme is the general word
For a table: boş masa var mı?
Fiyat is the price of a thing
Nakit mi, kart mı?
Pays for every bus, tram, metro and ferry; top it up at a kiosk or machine, and one card can pay for several people
Döviz bürosu = exchange office

items.en: how much will you let it go for?
items.note: Son fiyat ne? = what's your final price?
Bargaining is for bazaars and carpet shops, not for shops with price tags
Bozuk para = change; drivers ask Bozuğunuz var mı?
Just cep in speech
Phone charge is şarj
Telefon çekmiyor = there's no signal
People also just say app
Said 'onlayn'; çevrimiçi is the official word
Klimayı kıs = turn it down
Aman! = careful / oh dear
The standard consolation
Öylesine sordum = I just asked
-mış adds 'apparently, I've just learned this' – how you react to news
Bulamıyorum = I can't find it
No word like lakh – Turkish counts in bin and milyon
At bayram you kiss the hand and touch it to your forehead; they give you money or sweets
Shoes off, shoulders covered, women cover their hair; avoid prayer times
Bana kızma = don't be cross with me
Korkma = don't be scared
Gülümsemek = to smile
Değişmek = to change by itself
To a driver or waiter it means keep the change
Şarkı söylemek = to sing; türkü = folk song
Also used as 'but, only'
Ne bileyim = how should I know

items.en: could you put the meter on?
items.note: Ask before you set off
With harmony: -ıncı/-inci/-uncu/-üncü
Hour takes -e: altıya çeyrek kala
Işıklardan sağa dönün = turn right at the lights
112 for all emergencies
Sağa dönün = turn right; same verb as 'to return', and the root of döner
Turkish has no relative pronoun; it builds a participle on the verb
Often Ne yapalım, olan oldu
Also the verb for driving: araba kullanmak
Numbers just stack; no special word
Dört loses its t before the suffix
Tatil = holiday

items.en: dates: plain cardinal + month, never an ordinal

items.note: Also means the hob
Eşim is the neutral choice, karım the direct one; bare karı sounds coarse
Nişanlı = engaged, fiancé(e)
Same word as son-in-law; gelin likewise covers bride and daughter-in-law
In the street you address any older person as amca or teyze
Of things, eski
Kemiksiz = boneless
One word covers bitter, spicy-hot and painful; context decides
Tadına bakar mısınız? – market sellers say it constantly
No single word for a quarter-kilo: say 250 gram
Also the month January
'Poşet ister misiniz?' is asked at every till and it is charged for. A cloth one is a bez torba.
The electric kind is a termosifon
Terliyorum = I'm sweating
Otobüse binmek; inmek = to get off
Until about midday; after that İyi günler

What a waiter or host opens with; Ne içersiniz? for drinks

items.en: don't let it get to you
items.note: Merak etme = don't worry
Seni özledim = I miss you
Also an engaged phone line: hat meşgul
Boş = free/empty; bedava = free of charge
Mesleğiniz ne? = what do you do?
Dersler nasıl gidiyor?
Lise = secondary school
A national obsession and a very safe conversation topic
Football; the big three are Galatasaray, Fenerbahçe and Beşiktaş
Haberleri izliyoruz
Şunu tutar mısın? = could you hold this? Also 'to hire or rent': ev tutmak, taksi tutmak. Booking a seat is yer ayırtmak (hs-1024).
Telefonum düştü = I dropped my phone
İkram olsun / benden olsun = it's on the house / on me
Birine sor = ask someone; biriyle = with someone
Evdedir = he'll be at home – the -dır suffix does the same guessing job
Speech often just uses the present: şimdi çıkıyorum
Güzelce = nicely; the -ce suffix builds adverbs
The Turkish host's line; you'll hear it every visit

items.en: let me know when you get there
items.note: Haber vermek = to let someone know
Aferin sana = well done you
Praising a child, add maşallah – doing without it is thought to invite bad luck
Shoes come off at the door and you're handed a pair
The two big holidays are Ramazan (Şeker) and Kurban Bayramı; greet people with İyi bayramlar
Kimlik = ID card, which hotels ask for
Evlilik yıl dönümü = wedding anniversary
Güneş gözlüğü = sunglasses; gözlükçü = optician

items.en: the yes/no question word: Geliyor musun? = are you coming?
items.note: Nothing else marks a yes/no question. Written separately, harmonised four ways, and it carries the person ending: İngiliz misiniz?, geliyor musun?, var mı?

items.en: every suffix copies the last vowel of the word it lands on
items.note: Two-way: e after e i ö ü, a after a ı o u – evde, masada. Four-way: evim, kızım, okulum, gözüm. Learn this once and every suffix in the course follows.

items.word: verb last, no articles, no gender
items.en: word order: everything comes before the verb, and there is no 'the'
items.note: Ben yarın İstanbul'a gidiyorum – the verb ends the sentence. 'bir' does the work of 'a' when you need it; there is no word for 'the' at all.

items.word: c ç ş ı ö ü ğ
items.roman: c ç ş ı ö ü ğ
items.en: the seven letters English hasn't got
items.note: c = English j (cami = 'jah-mee'), ç = ch, ş = sh, ı = the vowel in 'butter', ö and ü as in French, ğ is silent and just stretches the vowel before it.

items.en: object marker – used only when the object is a definite one
items.note: Kitap okudum = I read a book; Kitabı okudum = I read the book. Names and bu/şu/o always take it: Ahmet'i gördüm, bunu aldım.

items.en: noun + noun compounds put -(s)i on the second word
items.note: How half the menu and every sign is built: elma çayı, yatak odası, mercimek çorbası, baş ağrısı, cep telefonu. The first word stays bare.

items.en: final p ç t k soften to b c d ğ when a vowel follows
items.note: Kitap/kitabı, ağaç/ağacı, kanat/kanadı, ekmek/ekmeği, renk/rengi. Nothing happens before a consonant: kitapta.
Plain infinitive plus istemek. Question: Görmek ister misiniz? Negative: gitmek istemiyorum. The noun version is separate: bir çay istiyorum.
The traveller's workhorse question: Boş oda var mı?, Etsiz bir şey var mı?, Yer var mı? The answer comes back var or yok.
Said walking into a shop and again walking out, roughly midday to dusk. Günaydın before that, İyi akşamlar after.
On arrival in the evening. İyi geceler is for leaving, or for bed.

items.en: goodbye – the one leaving says Hoşça kalın, the one staying says Güle güle
items.note: Turkish splits goodbye by who is moving, so you almost never say the same word back. To a friend: Hoşça kal.

items.en: the fixed reply to Hoş geldiniz
items.note: You are welcomed into every shop, home and hotel. This is the answer, and there is no other one.
The standard reply to teşekkür ederim. 'Bir şey değil' and 'Ne demek' do the same job more casually.
Religious in origin, secular in daily use – it mostly means 'fingers crossed', and it turns up in almost every plan anyone makes.

items.en: touch wood; how lovely (about a child or good news)
items.note: Praising a baby without it is thought to invite the evil eye. Pair it up: Maşallah, çok tatlı.
The sneezer answers 'Sen de gör' or 'Hep beraber'.

items.en: not at all; you're too kind
items.note: Said 'estafurullah'. The reply when someone praises you, or apologises to you for nothing.
What a driver asks; you answer with -e: Sultanahmet'e, lütfen. The set is nerede, nereye, nereden.

items.en: counter word: bir tane = one of them
items.note: Şundan iki tane, lütfen. The noun stays singular after a number: iki tane çay, üç tane simit.
The pair that orders your food and drink. Both harmonise: acılı/acısız, buzlu/buzsuz, tuzlu/tuzsuz.
Adana is the hot one, Urfa the mild one; şiş is on a skewer, İskender comes on bread under yoghurt.
Ekmek arası = in bread, dürüm = in a wrap, porsiyon = on a plate with rice. From dönmek, to turn.
Izgara köfte with piyaz (bean salad) is the standard lokanta plate.

items.en: menemen (eggs cooked down with tomato and pepper)
items.note: The hot half of a Turkish breakfast. Ordered sucuklu (with sausage) or sade.
Bir bira, lütfen. Efes and Bomonti are what you'll be offered; büyük or küçük for the size.
Taken with water and ice alongside meze and fish, over a long evening. 'Şerefe!' = cheers.
Kırmızı = red, beyaz = white; a glass is bir kadeh.
Same frame for anything: Telefonum çalındı, Cüzdanım çalındı. The police station is a karakol.
The hospital sign to look for is 'Acil Servis'. 112 covers ambulance, fire and police.
Answer with the number plus -yım: kırk yaşındayım. Asked as freely as 'are you married?'
Sigara içmek = to smoke, with the same verb as drinking. Indoors it's banned everywhere, which is why every café has pavement tables.
The word on the signs you need to read: Sigara içmek yasaktır, Girmek yasak, Fotoğraf çekmek yasak.
Deniz kenarı = the seafront. In Istanbul the water you cross is the Boğaz, the Bosphorus.
Müzekart is the annual pass. 'Saat kaçta kapanıyor?' = what time does it close?
Dahil = included. 'KDV dahil' on a menu means the VAT is already in the price.

items.en: now, from now on; (with a negative) not any more
items.note: Artık gitmem lazım = I really should go now; Artık yok = there's none left. On its own, 'Yok artık!' = you're joking.
Zaten biliyordum = I knew anyway. One of the commonest words in spoken Turkish, and it rarely translates cleanly.
Follows the word it emphasises: Ben bile bilmiyorum = even I don't know.
Hemen geliyorum = I'll be right there; hemen şurada = just over there.

items.en: the meal that breaks the Ramadan fast
items.note: Sahur is the pre-dawn one. During Ramazan the restaurants fill at sunset, and being asked along is a compliment.
Literally 'coffee-coloured'. Mor = purple, gri = grey.
Plain infinitive plus için. After a noun, için follows the bare word: senin için, bunun için.

items.en: where the stress falls, and the three things that move it
items.note: Default is the final syllable: kaPI, geliYOR. Place names break it (İSTANbul, ANkara), the negative pulls it back (GELmedim), and the question word is never stressed.
